pivot.text: You see, that rushing water is the tide.

last.text: The king thought Yi had nothing left, but he had one line and a sea that switched sides.

sentences.text: Told to give up the navy, Admiral Yi answered with one line and sailed thirteen ships at a hundred and thirty-three.
His captains thought he was mad.
You see, Japan's invasion fleet has just wiped out Korea's navy.
Yi's ships are all that's left.
So when the king tells him to give up the navy, Yi answers: "I still have ships."
But the Japanese fleet fills the horizon.
So Yi picks his spot: a strait so narrow the huge fleet has to squeeze through it.
Locals call it the crying strait, for the sound of its water.
The Japanese pour in, carried by that rushing water.
Ship after ship after ship.
His captains hang back, happy to let the admiral go first.
The strait is so tight only a few Japanese ships can reach Yi at once, and his cannons hold them off.
You see, that rushing water is the tide.
Every few hours, it stops and runs the other way.
Historians who rebuilt that day's tides think the tide turned mid-battle.
Now the water runs back out.
The front Japanese ships get shoved back into their own ships, and the tangle is stuck in front of Yi's cannons.
Korean records count thirty-one Japanese ships lost, and none of Yi's.
The rest turn back.
Suddenly, his captains can't wait to follow him.
The king thought Yi had nothing left, but he had one line and a sea that switched sides.
